title: Wishes About the Past: Ojalá Hubiera and ¡Quién Hubiera!

sections.title: What you know
sections.content: You know *ojalá* with the present subjunctive from B1 Unit 3, for a wish that can still come true, and *ojalá* with the imperfect subjunctive from B2 Unit 15, for a wish that is not true now. A wish about the past, about something that did not happen, takes the pluperfect subjunctive: *Ojalá hubiera estudiado más* "I wish I had studied more". It is a regret: the wish can no longer come true.

sections.title: Three wishes with ojalá
rows: I hope I have time tomorrow. (it can still happen)
I wish I had more time. (it is not true now)
I wish I had had more time. (it did not happen)
I wish it had not rained.

sections.title: ¡Quién hubiera…!
sections.content: You can also say a past wish with *quién*: *¡Quién hubiera estado allí!* "If only I had been there!" Here *quién* stands for "I": the speaker wishes it for themselves. This form is less common than *ojalá* in everyday speech, and you will meet it more in writing and in emotional exclamations.

items.english: I wish we had left earlier.
I wish you had told me.
I wish I had not said that.
If only I had been there!
If only I had known it before!

sections.content: Use *hubiera* (or *hubiese*), never *habría*, after *ojalá*: say *Ojalá hubiera venido*, not *Ojalá habría venido*. A wish about the past is always a regret, so it often goes with words like *antes* or *a tiempo*.
